https://english.radio.cz/senate-urges-fa.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Senate urges faster rollout of EU disability card Facebook Twitter The Czech Senate has called on the government to speed up preparations for the introduction of European disability cards so that Czech people with disabilities can begin using them within a year. Senators made the recommendation while discussing the EU Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2030. The relevant EU directive must be transposed into Czech law by June 5 next year. The Senate also urged the government to clarify how the new European disability card will relate to the country's existing disability ID cards. Labour and Social Affairs Minister Aleš Juchelka said the European Disability Card, together with the European Parking Card, is intended to make it easier for people with disabilities to travel and move freely across the European Union. Photograph: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP/Getty Images Global development UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’ Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze Supported by About this content Mark Townsend Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.07 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days. A year after the fall of El Fasher , the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city. A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze . The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”. During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century . Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for. The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF. Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings. Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed. Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city. A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken. A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.” During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war. The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack. https://talkingpointsmemo.com/news/a-bal.text: News A Ballroom Donor, a Sanctions Waiver, $201 Million in Public Money: The Mystery of Konstantin Sokolov by Josh Kovensky 10.13.26 | 11:26 am Konstantin Sokolov at a Geoeconomics Roundtable hosted by the Munich Security Conference in 2025 in Washington, DC. Source: MSC/Simon 16 Ever since he contributed to the White House ballroom project last year, things have gone well for Konstantin A. Sokolov: the Treasury Department gave a company he manages a license to get around international sanctions against Russia. The State Department appointed him to run a $201 million foreign investment fund in the Caucasus. And, per sources familiar, he convened meetings to discuss investments related to Donald Trump Jr.’s VC firm, 1789 Capital. It’s a remarkable winning streak for the Russian-American investor, who, until 2025, had a meager public history of political giving. Per records obtained by TPM through FOIA, a Texas company for which Sokolov is listed as manager called Dynamic Frontier Holdings LLC first applied for a license from the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Asset Controls on October 27, 2025. OFAC issued the license around 10 weeks later, on Jan. 5, a timeline experts described to TPM as remarkably quick. The company used the license in June to buy a copper mine in Armenia previously owned by VTB Bank, according to a July Radio Liberty report . The Treasury Department had sanctioned VTB as Russia launched its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, describing it as a “critical artery of Russia’s financial system” through which Moscow financed its war effort. The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists first reported the license’s issuance. Over the past year, Sokolov has become a prolific political donor. He was listed by the White House as a contributor to the ballroom project days before Dynamic Frontier Holdings applied for the license. The amount he donated to the ballroom project has not been disclosed. He also, during the second Trump presidency, gave $12 million to a Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., as well as hundreds of thousands of dollars to the National Republican Senatorial Committee, and $100,000 in support of Sens. Susan Collins (R-ME) and $120,000 for Pete Ricketts (R-NE). Since 2025, he has given more than $14 million to Republican causes, according to FEC records. Before that, his only contributions were in 2008: a combined $3,600 to Barack Obama and a PAC supporting him. Over the last several months, the Trump administration not only opened the door for Sokolov’s business deal with VTB Bank, it also placed Sokolov in an influential position in the Caucasus. This summer, the State Department placed Sokolov in charge of a $201 million Trans-Caspian enterprise fund set to invest public money in the south Caucasus, a region that includes Armenia, as part of a “Trump road” initiative. The Guardian broke that news in July. The fund exists to help provide access for the United States to raw materials used in microchips and the construction of AI data centers, regional experts told TPM. The fund and associated projects could allow resources from Central Asia and the Caucasus an easier path westward, towards the United States. “He hardly would be my first choice,” Daniel Fried, a former State Department sanctions coordinator who worked on a similar fund in Poland, said of the Trans-Caspian Enterprise fund. Fried added that Sokolov having business interests in Armenia while running a fund devoted to investing public money in companies in the region could present an issue: “You have to ask yourself whether his involvement in [the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund] is going to lead to conflicts of interests.” In addition to the acquisition of the copper mine, Armenia’s second largest, Sokolov has deepened his personal business investments in Armenia and Europe more broadly in recent years. In 2024, he and Zhe Zhang, co-investor who was described in securities filings as a former employee of MOFCOM, China’s Ministry of Commerce, acquired a stake in an Armenian telecommunications operator. They did so via a Cyprus company called Fedilco, the company said . Another project appears to have intersected with the Trump family. A Gibraltar data center project called Pelagos lists Sokolov as its chairman; a representative of the company met with Donald Trump Jr. while he was visiting the enclave last year, per local press reports . Around the same time, Sokolov convened a meeting to discuss foreign investments related to 1789 Capital, the investment firm where the president’s son is a partner, according to two people familiar with the trip. One of the people said Don Jr. attended. It’s unclear whether any investments — into 1789 Capital, or by 1789 Capital — resulted from the trip; both sources said that 1789 Capital does not invest in non-U.S. companies. Sokolov, 51, has little in the way of a publicly documented business career before 2025, when he made a $100 million gift to the University of Chicago Booth School of Business. Sokolov is an alumnus of Booth’s Executive MBA program, and one of the only descriptions of his work over the last two decades comes from a 2014 article in the school’s alumni magazine, which describes him running an investment firm in Russia alongside a business partner, a fellow Booth alumnus who had previously worked in high-level roles at Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska’s massive conglomerate, Basic Element. A spokesperson for Sokolov didn’t return a request to make him available for an interview, and argued strenuously that there’s no conflict of interest in Sokolov’s activities related to the Trans-Caspian enterprise fund and that there’s no connection between his political contributions and the license that Treasury issued for the acquisition of the Armenian copper mine. The spokesperson also argued to TPM that we had confused aspects of Sokolov’s biography with that of another person with a similar name, Konstantin Borisovich Sokolov. TPM found that there are, in fact, two high-profile Konstantin Borisovich Sokolovs. One is a former managing director of Deripaska’s company, Basic Element, and was reportedly born in the late 1960s. The other Konstantin Borisovich Sokolov appears to be an alias used by Konstantin Kudryavtsev, an alleged Russian security services officer under Treasury sanctions for his purported involvement in the poisoning of Alexei Navalny. Per Russian naming conventions, a patronymic is derived from the father’s first name. Neither of the other Sokolovs share the ballroom donor’s patronymic — Anatolyevich. Nor do they share Konstantin A. Sokolov’s birth year — 1975. Neither of the other two appear to have attended the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business. Konstantin A. Sokolov’s spokesperson didn’t return a follow-up request for comment about which aspects of this story they believe corresponds to the wrong Sokolov. “Mr. Sokolov is a U.S. citizen and complies with all applicable laws and regulations,” the person said in a statement. Chicago and Russia Sokolov appears to have had little public profile before 2025. Several news outlets have described him as a newcomer to political giving, listing him among other brand-new entrants to the world of MAGA political contributions. NBC noted in January that Sokolov had gone “from making a handful of four-figure donations in the past to dropping more than $11 million into MAGA Inc.’s coffers in just one year.” He largely emerged into the public eye in 2025, with his $100 million donation to the University of Chicago. In an interview with the Chicago Tribune , Sokolov estimated the gift at nearly 10% of his overall wealth. “Chicago Booth played a very important role in my life,” Sokolov told the newspaper. “The business school served as a foundation of my career success and then my success as an entrepreneur.” Sokolov was elected to the university’s board of trustees in August. Over the last year and a half, Sokolov has also become a player at the Munich Security Conference. The group listed him as having participated in its February 2025 event; in January 2026, the conference announced that he had given a major contribution to its foundation. Before 2025, details of Sokolov’s life are sparse. TPM found some evidence of a life — social media profiles, an account on a wine-ranking website. But the answer to how and where Sokolov gained his apparently immense wealth remains unclear. Originally from St. Petersburg, Russia, Sokolov first immigrated to the United States in 1997, settling in Ohio. He eventually moved to Denver, before receiving an Executive MBA from Booth in 2005. He seems to have lived in Chicago until the late 2000s; a biography on his website says that he worked for a British gas firm during this time. By 2011, records obtained by TPM show, Sokolov faced foreclosure on a condo he owned in downtown Chicago. When a process server tried to deliver Sokolov a copy of a complaint in a separate case relating to unpaid condo fees on the unit, he was, according to court documents, told by another resident that Sokolov was living in Moscow, Russia. Documents filed in the 2011 fees case refer to Sokolov as “Konstantin A. Sokolov.” The case ended in a default judgment; Cook County Sheriffs sold the unit, the docket says . That same year, Sokolov appears to have deepened a business career in Europe via the founding of an investment firm called Gotthard; Sokolov described himself as the founder and chairman of the company in a later SEC filing . Swiss corporate records from the firm’s 2011 incorporation described Sokolov as a “Russian citizen living in Moscow,” per a translation from the German. An archived version of the 2014 Booth alumni magazine story also suggests that Sokolov, described as a 2005 Booth graduate, worked in Russia for several years. Per the story, Sokolov founded an investment firm in Russia called IFG Basis in 2008 along with a business partner, Evgeny Tonkacheev. The story describes Tonkacheev as a dual physics and math PhD who in the early 2000s was CEO of Basic Element, the massive industrial conglomerate belonging to Deripaska, the Russian oligarch. A LinkedIn profile for Tonkacheev lists him as having worked as a CEO and managing director at Basic Element at the time. Deripaska is largely known in the United States for his financial ties to 2016 Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort who, prosecutors found, offered Deripaska private briefings and information about the Trump campaign via an intermediary. A Senate Intelligence Committee report identified the intermediary as a Russian intelligence officer. Tonkacheev left Basic Element for Booth, the 2014 alumni magazine story says. “I had no special business education but got a lot of experience working for this big company,” the story quoted Tonkacheev as saying. Russian business news reports from the period describe IFG Basis as seeking to invest in Russian real estate and industry; one news report quoted Sokolov as saying he wanted to build a “five star hotel” in St. Petersburg’s historic center. By 2021, it appears Sokolov’s business activities had returned to the United States. Gotthard moved to dissolve itself that year, corporate filings show, and Sokolov had embarked on a Wall Street career through involvement in two SPACs, publicly traded shell companies used to raise capital to buy privately held firms. That appears not to have lasted. In August 2021, Sokolov was listed in securities filings as the chair of the audit committee of Alpha Star Acquisition Corp., one of the SPACs. The committee’s responsibilities included hiring auditors and reviewing issues that might affect the company’s financial statements. He left in October 2022 . The company later merged with an Estonian fintech firm, but it also ran into some difficulties: in 2024, it told investors that its financial statements for 2021 and 2022 could no longer be relied upon. It had overstated its assets by $118,228,816. In 2024, a Cypriot company called Fedilco acquired an Armenian telecommunications operator called Viva, according to a Viva press release. The announcement described Sokolov as an investor who was Fedilco’s “ultimate beneficiary” along with a businessman named Zhe Zhang, described in SEC filings as a former employee of MOFCOM, the abbreviation for China’s Ministry of Commerce. Viva’s previous owner was Mobile TeleSystems PJSC, MTS, a Russian conglomerate subject to international sanctions. From Trumpworld to Armenia The Viva acquisition came months after fighting drew to a halt in Armenia’s war with Azerbaijan, which had been ongoing for years but flared up in 2023. Armenia had long relied on Russia for its security but, bogged down in Ukraine, the Russian government declined to intervene. This left the country seeking American help. In August 2025, President Trump announced a peace deal to end the conflict: the two countries would gain peace through trade, he said. The U.S. would create an Armenian development company (74 percent of the company’s shares would belong to Washington) and would sponsor a “Trump road” to knit the two previously warring nations together. As part of this, the State Department agreed to create what it now calls a Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund. The U.S. government created similar funds across the former Eastern Bloc after the fall of communism and in the Middle East: the idea is to have the U.S. government invest in companies and projects that might speed along development. Projects launched as part of the initiative are largely focused on AI . U.S. officials have said that the project’s purpose is to create a “middle corridor,” allowing rare earths and other resources to make their way from Central Asia westwards while avoiding Iran, Russia, and China. The Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund was incorporated in Delaware in January 2026, corporate records show. The State Department appointed Sokolov as its chairman this year, and granted the fund $201 million. Federal records reviewed by TPM show that a Chicago attorney listed on several of Sokolov’s private businesses serves as the fund’s point of contact. The fund has said that it holds itself to the highest governance and ethical standards in compliance with U.S. laws and those of the countries in which it operates. The fund is registered at an address whose listed owner is a Miami real estate agent who advertises his “discretion” and “distinguished reputation advising ultra-high-net-worth individuals, international investors.” Dynamic Frontier Holdings, the company that acquired the copper mine, is listed at the same address. Dynamic Frontier Holdings’ corporate registration The Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund’s registration in a federal contracting database. TPM sought more information about the $201 million the State Department granted to the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund; congressional staffers said that because the money came from a recently created “National Security Investment Programs” account, it would have minimal oversight. The president has vast authority over national security matters; so long as the State Department claims the investments are national security-related, Congress receives limited updates, they said. TPM sought comment from as many people and entities as it could find that are tied to Sokolov. Some didn’t return our requests; others replied, only to describe our questions as having to do with information that is already public, and therefore not necessary to address, or information that is private, and therefore not subject to discussion. UChicago didn’t respond to questions about Sokolov’s contributions to the school. The White House didn’t return a request for comment. Pelagos Data Centres declined to comment; Viva Armenia, the telecom asset tied to Sokolov, told TPM that the company had “received all necessary authorizations from Armenia’s regulatory bodies.” The State Department initially acknowledged TPM’s request, before failing to

https://www.rigzone.com/news/equinor_bag.text: SUBSCRIBE SEARCH ARTICLES NEWS Equinor Bags New Contract to Supply Dutch with Norwegian Gas by Jov Onsat | Rigzone Staff | Tuesday, October 13, 2026 | 11:42 AM EST Equinor and Eneco have now signed three agreements this year for gas supply to the Netherlands and Germany. Image by FOTOFORCE via iStock Equinor ASA has signed a new five-year agreement to export about 9 terawatt hours (nearly 32 billion cubic feet) of natural gas to power and gas utility Eneco for supply to the Netherlands. Deliveries to the Dutch gas grid under the new contract, on top of a five-year supply agreed earlier this year, started October 1, according to separate statements by Rotterdam-based Eneco and Norway's majority state-owned Equinor. The gas will be supplied to Dutch residential and small business customers, Eneco said. "In the current geopolitical situation, Eneco aims to contribute to a secure and reliable energy supply for Europe. Norwegian gas plays an important role in this, as is evident from this long-standing collaboration between Equinor and Eneco", Eneco said. Eneco supplies electricity, natural gas and heat in the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and the United Kingdom. "The contracted Norwegian gas has the benefit of having an 11.8 percent lower CO2e footprint from production and transport compared to the average Dutch natural gas supplied in 2025 to residential and business customers through the G-gas network", Eneco added. "This is mainly because the gas under the contract is produced and transported using renewable power from shore and delivered by pipeline to the Netherlands, rather than as liquefied natural gas transported by tankers". Equinor and Eneco have now signed three gas supply agreements this year, all with verified environmental attributes or guarantees of origin through Attributes SA's platform, according to Equinor. Advertisement - Scroll to continue Under the earlier agreement for the supply of gas produced in the Norwegian continental shelf to the Netherlands, yearly deliveries of up to 500 million cubic meters began February. The third agreement, also lasting five years, is for supply to Germany. "The agreement runs until the end of 2030 and covers annual volumes of around 2.2 terawatt‑hours (around 0.2 bcm/year), and deliveries to Germany started in April 2026", Equinor said May 19. "The gas supplied under the agreement has a greenhouse gas intensity lower than alternative supply into the German grid". Separately, Equinor has secured a 15-year agreement with Uniper to supply over 30 TWh - about 2.8 billion cubic meters - a year of natural gas to Germany. "Germany is Equinor's largest market for natural gas and has been an anchor market for Norwegian gas since exports started in 1977. Deliveries under the new agreement will start on 1 January 2027, the same year Norway and Equinor mark 50 years of gas exports to Germany", Equinor said August 24. "Pricing will reflect market terms, while other commercial details are confidential between the parties", Equinor said. Concurrently Equinor and Uniper signed a letter of intent "to explore possible sales from Equinor to Uniper of sustainability-related attributes linked to supplies under the new gas sales agreement", it added. Also in August Equinor announced an agreement to export crude to several European countries via ORLEN SA. The Polish majority state-owned company committed to buying more than nine million metric tons a year of oil for three years from Norway. Equinor is to supply the oil from the Johan Sverdrup field to ORLEN's refineries in Poland, Lithuania and Czechia starting September 2026, Equinor announced August 20. "The agreement also allows for the possibility of supplying other crude grades produced from fields on the Norwegian continental shelf", Equinor said. Ireneusz Fąfara, president of ORLEN's management board, said ORLEN expects Norway to account for up to one-quarter of the company's yearly demand. "This agreement is a concrete response to global market instability and demonstrates that resilience in the energy sector is built through long-term cooperation with partners that provide predictable supplies and operational reliability", Fąfara said. Photograph: Achol Arok/The Guardian View image in fullscreen On Wednesday, police found a sofa containing a human torso located about five metres off the roadway at Lane Cove North in Sydney’s lower north shore. Photograph: Achol Arok/The Guardian Sydney Human torso found in sofa in Sydney bushland prompts homicide investigation Police called to Lane Cove North on Wednesday after sofa found containing human torso believed to be that of adult man Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Achol Arok Wed 11 Nov 2026 20.27 EST First published on Wed 11 Nov 2026 16.09 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New South Wales police have entered their second day searching for remains after a human torso was found in bushland on Sydney’s lower north shore. Police were called to Lane Cove North about 2.30pm on Wednesday after recieving “a number of reports from members of the public” regarding a strong odour in the area, Supt Paul Devaney told media on Thursday morning. Officers found a sofa containing human remains consisting of “a torso … devoid of head, arms and legs” about five metres off the roadway, Devaney said. There were signs the body, believed to be that of an adult male, had been there for “at least a couple of days”. Map The quiet suburban street remained cordoned off to locals who watched several police cars and detectives line the narrow street on Thursday morning. Groups of officers were deployed to conduct ground searches. Local resident Rodney Campbell said he walks his dog, Mochi, “pretty much every day along this street”. The 60-year-old said he knew something was wrong when he saw police scouting his usual walking route on Wednesday afternoon. “There was two cars and there was one policeman there, the others were presumably in the bush,” he said. “I’m a bit shocked, I guess, because this doesn’t happen in this area. It’s usually very quiet here.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Campbell grimaced as he tried to describe the “very strong smell”, and said “yesterday was the first day we smelled it”. “I assumed it actually was a dead animal. I’ve smelled it on farms and things before, like a dead cow or something. But not one that’s just been recently dead, I’m talking one that’s been dead for a very long time.” View image in fullscreen Supt Paul Devaney said police didn’t believe there was any ongoing threat to the public. Photograph: Morgan Reinwald/AAP Campbell has lived in the area for almost 30 years and said the bushland has often been a problem for illegal dumping “because it’s steep” and “goes down” off the street. “Stuff does get dumped here … just rubbish, the sort of stuff that people would throw away and don’t want to take to the tip,” he said. Amthea, another local who requested her full name not be published, was also walking her dog on Thursday morning. She said it was “very scary and out of character for this area”, and that she could remember only “one other major incident” in the 21 years she had lived there. “I’m very surprised. It’s generally a very quiet area. Many of us walk those bushes every day, often by ourselves with our dogs. My daughter does walk there almost daily,” she said. “So I just would like to understand what happened, so that we can feel comfortable continuing to use the bushes.” Detectives together with the state’s homicide squad launched an investigation, with the Aviation Command (PolAir) and cadaver dog deployed. Members of the public with information, including dashcam or security camera footage that may be relevant, were urged to contact police with information. Devaney sought to reassure Lane Cove residents that there was no apparent threat to locals. “There is no indication that this person met foul play within the area of Lane Cove. But it is very early stages in the investigation and we are still undertaking numerous and comprehensive inquiries,” he said.
